title: Three refineries in three nights, and a fight over mines in Hormuz
summary: Ukraine's renewed refinery campaign, Russia's strikes on Dnipro and the power grid, the US–Iran standoff over Hormuz mine claims ahead of the midterms, Houthi attacks on Aden, and why a third US carrier may be heading to the Middle East.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Welcome to the ForceFinder Daily Briefing. I'm Avery.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And I'm Cole. Quick note before we start: this show is generated automatically from the open-source reporting behind the ForceFinder map, so think of it as a guided tour of today's update, not as the final word. Every story we mention has source links on the map.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Right. And today is the first of November, and honestly, there's a theme running through a lot of this. Energy. Oil refineries, power grids, tankers. It's all about who can squeeze whose energy supply.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: So let's start in Russia, because the numbers there are striking. Ukraine had reportedly paused its long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries for about two weeks, under pressure from Washington. That pause is clearly over.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Three refineries in three nights.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Exactly. On October thirtieth, drones set the Novokuybyshevsk refinery in Samara region on fire. Local authorities said two people died responding to the fires. The next night it was the Bashneft Novoil refinery in Ufa, although that one hasn't been independently confirmed. And overnight into today, the Lukoil refinery at Kstovo, near Nizhny Novgorod, plus the power plant next to it.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And Ukrainian outlet United twenty-four estimates those three plants together are something like ten percent of Russia's refining capacity. Russia has opened a terrorism case over the Kstovo attack, and its defence ministry says it shot down two hundred and thirty-five Ukrainian drones overnight.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: There was also a strike on a plant in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, in Rostov region, that makes solid rocket fuel. Ukraine's General Staff says Neptune missiles and drones set a warehouse on fire and damaged four workshops. And this comes a few days after two huge drone waves at Moscow, six hundred and thirteen drones one night and eight hundred and sixty-two the next, according to the mayor, which shut down the city's airports.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And Russia's strikes on Ukraine have been just as heavy. The worst single incident this week was in Dnipro. On October twenty-ninth, a jet-powered drone hit a platform at the main train station, while a train to Zaporizhzhia was stopped there. Officials put the death toll at fourteen to fifteen, including five railway workers.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Same day, a missile strike in central Chernihiv killed two fifteen-year-old girls, and drones hit an apartment block in Kremenchuk. Then overnight into today, President Zelensky said strikes on substations and power lines in four regions, Dnipropetrovsk, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr and Khmelnytskyi, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: So that's the energy war in both directions. What about the front line itself?

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Ukraine's General Staff reported two hundred and sixty-four combat clashes in a single day, with the heaviest fighting around Pokrovsk, where it says fifty-five Russian assaults were pushed back. The Institute for the Study of War assesses that Russia has made gains near Huliaipole and Orikhiv in the south, while Ukraine has pushed forward south of Oleksandrivka.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And there's one small, hopeful thread. A local ceasefire around the occupied town of Oleshky, in Kherson region, brokered with US help, ran from October twenty-seventh to today. Both sides said it held, and it let aid convoys in and some residents out. On the bigger diplomatic track, the Kremlin has said it's open in principle to three-way talks with Ukraine and the US in mid-November.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Okay. Let's head south, to the Strait of Hormuz, because there's a real information fight going on there.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Yeah, this one's interesting. Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy says several tankers have hit sea mines in the strait over the last few days. The counts vary, three tankers, four tankers, depending on the outlet, and Iran says those ships were using what it calls unauthorized routes.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: And US Central Command flatly disputes that. Admiral Brad Cooper said on October thirtieth that American minesweeping has cleared the main transit lanes. A Central Command spokesman went further, saying Iran's mine claims are false and that Iran is using missiles and drones instead. The Associated Press couldn't confirm the Iranian tanker claims.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: But ships really have been damaged. A tanker called the Louise One caught fire after limpet mines were attached to its hull, and Oman says it rescued twenty-five sailors from a burning ship. And traffic through the strait is way down. One monitor counted just two commercial transits on October thirty-first.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Meanwhile, the politics. On Saturday, President Trump told reporters the US still has one or two Iranian sites to take care of, naming a suspected underground nuclear site, and said that could be done in ten minutes. Secretary of State Rubio, though, said no decision has been made on new strikes. US officials have reportedly told regional allies to be ready for possible renewed action after Tuesday's midterm elections.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And Iran's foreign minister says Tehran and Qatari mediators are working on a plan to reopen the strait within two days, but only if Washington meets Iran's conditions. So far, he says, no breakthrough.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Which brings us neatly to the ships, because the US naval picture in that region could be about to change. Right now there are two carriers in the Arabian Sea, the George Washington and the George H. W. Bush.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And the Theodore Roosevelt just finished exercise Keen Sword with Japan. The Makin Island amphibious group, with the thirteenth Marine Expeditionary Unit, pulled into Yokosuka on October twenty-sixth. Fox News, citing US officials, reported that both groups are headed for the Middle East.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: Which, if it happens, would mean three carrier groups and two amphibious groups in Central Command's area sometime in November. The Navy hasn't announced that, so treat it as reported, not confirmed.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Let's do a quick lap of the other fronts. Yemen. The Houthis fired ballistic missiles at the presidential palace and the airport in Aden on October thirtieth. That's the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government. Saudi Arabia says it intercepted a Houthi drone near Mecca the same day, which the Houthis deny, and another drone near Riyadh on Saturday.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: In Gaza, medics say Israeli airstrikes today in al-Mawasi and in Gaza City's al-Rimal neighbourhood killed eight people, including five police officers. The Israeli military had no immediate comment. And in southern Lebanon, Israeli shelling continues around towns like Mayfadoun and Majdal Zoun, despite the June ceasefire.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: And in the South China Sea, China says it ran what it calls readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal, in response to Philippine actions.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: One last thing, for anyone using the map itself. ForceFinder now has two new layers. One shows the areas where groups the US designates as terrorist organizations are based, like Hezbollah, Hamas, the Houthis and al-Shabaab. The other shows major Russian, Chinese, North Korean and Iranian military sites, like fleet headquarters and the Spratly island bases.

segments.speaker: Avery
segments.text: Both are broad, approximate and sourced, just like everything else on the globe. So, the things to watch this week: the US midterms on Tuesday and whatever follows for Iran, whether that third carrier really heads west, and whether those mid-November Ukraine talks come together.

segments.speaker: Cole
segments.text: That's the briefing. Thanks for listening, and we'll see you tomorrow.
